cites.sentence: It capped increases within an existing tenancy but not the initial rent, and excluded SDUs with co-living services [D1p3].

Mrs Wong, nine years in an SDU with no written agreement, reports that the ordinance "changed nothing she can see" because the landlord still charges "whatever the market of desperate newcomers bears" [D4p1].
Mr Chan's rent of $5,800 consumes about a third of household income, and his worst experience was not price but two weeks' notice after requesting a window repair [D3p1].
SDU stock grew from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025, continuing through the ordinance, which suggests moderate regulation did not trigger visible stock exit [D2p1].
The academic literature explains why: second-generation controls — caps on increases within tenancies — show small or null effects on stock, and the 2021 ordinance is exactly that type [D6p2].
The Landlords Association's claim that members will exit if returns fall below mortgage cost [D5p2]
is asserted without data on actual margins, and its compliance-cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate [D5p3].
The visible stock stability may be an artifact of a non-binding instrument; a binding one behaves differently [D12p2].
The estimated elasticity of SDU-type supply to controlled rent levels is 0.31 to 0.48, meaning a 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].

In a modelled Hong Kong-like market, a 15 percent cut in initial rents transfers about $900 per month to incumbents while leaving 3,000 to 4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households [D6p4].

Berlin illustrates the same asymmetry: caps protect those already inside, and the bill is handed to those still outside — and when the Mietendeckel fell, suppressed increases released and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend [D7p2][D7p3].

Berlin illustrates the same asymmetry: caps protect those already inside, and the bill is handed to those still outside — and when the Mietendeckel fell, suppressed increases released and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend [D7p2][D7p3].
Inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based initial-rent cap would require a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years to stand up [D10p1].
Worse, the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong [D4p1], so enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail [D10p2].
Worse, the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong [D4p1], so enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail [D10p2].
The subcommittee could not identify any enforcement design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last [D10p3].
A hard cap would also invite compensation claims and judicial review, with a litigation timeline outlasting a Council term [D9p1][D9p3].
A hard cap would also invite compensation claims and judicial review, with a litigation timeline outlasting a Council term [D9p1][D9p3].
Counsel assesses that a cap on initial rent by reference to a published, indexed per-square-foot band can be defended as rate-capping rather than confiscation [D9p2].
This aligns with the NGO survey finding that 61 percent of tenants would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security of tenure, and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer [D11p1].
It also matches the government's own signaled direction: a "floor-standard + rent band" package rather than a hard cap, citing Berlin as a cautionary tale [D12p1].
The segment is tight because the queue is long, and every unit of enforcement capacity spent policing rents is a unit not spent inspecting fire, partition and ventilation conditions [D11p2].
Mr Chan himself names the waiting list, not rent, as what would help most [D3p3].
